extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature / professional scientists and scholars (early-20th-century researchers in physics, chemistry, astronomy, archaeology, and history)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for evaluating experimental claims, astronomical hypotheses, palaeontological observations, and historical/archaeological interpretations as found in correspondence, notes, and reviews in a scientific journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use purified materials to avoid contamination artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental investigations into radioactive products should start with purified uranium salts/compounds; commercial salts often contain appreciable amounts of other constituents which can give misleading indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a small proportion of an immediate parent substance in commercial salts is not evidence of a genetic connection; repeat tests on well-purified samples and report long-term measurements (example: a solution of purified uranium nitrate tested after more than two and a half years contained less than 10^-? gram of radium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-brief summaries that obscure meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, terse summary statements of results can be open to criticism and misinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When brevity risks ambiguity, provide a longer, more satisfactory summary that explicitly states the supported hypothesis and the limits of the conclusions (example: replace brief dismissal with a statement describing support for an hypothesis about intermediate products and the limited quantitative significance of another worker's results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require appropriate evidence before asserting genetic/causal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that one element (e.g., radium) is a disintegration product of another (e.g., uranium) should rely on strong, direct evidence rather than incidental associations in impure materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note what constitutes the only available evidence (in this case, constancy of the ratio between quantities in natural minerals) and be explicit about its limitations; avoid overstating causal conclusions from circumstantial data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate quantitative concentration in kinematic hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: For proposals that split a population into distinct kinematic systems (e.g., two 'drifts' of stars), it is not sufficient to show that some objects move forward and some backward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis must show a concentration of motions about two definite velocities (definite in magnitude and direction); models producing a continuous or haphazard distribution of velocities do not account for discrete double-drift observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare theoretical models directly with observed distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The viability of a dynamical or structural hypothesis is judged by how well its predicted distributions match observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue whether mechanisms (e.g., gravitation towards a universal centre) can produce the observed separations; if a model yields a smooth transition rather than concentrated groups, it likely fails to explain discrete empirical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use microscopic/developmental examination to resolve morphological succession questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of dental succession and homologies should be informed by careful microscopic study of developing teeth and germs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When surface or gross observations are inconclusive, undertake detailed micro-anatomical examination of embryonic/developing structures to clarify succession and homology (the author proposes immediate microscopic study to obtain further light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspect 'arrested solar dates' for fairs and festivals between 10th–20th of quarter months
rubrics_metrics.description: Any dates between the 10th and the 20th in March, June, September, and December may indicate an 'arrested solar day' (a date retained from an earlier solar/seasonal calendar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams/calculations of calendar drift since key epochs (e.g., Council of Nice or the start of the Julian year) to infer the period when a fair or festival was instituted; treat such dates as hypotheses to be corroborated by other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret legends and later accounts cautiously; seek corroborating cultural/archaeological evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Legendary narratives (e.g., saint lives) often disguise older ritual or solar symbolism; do not accept later attributions of significance without cross-evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare bardic records, stone-circle usage, festival timing, and other archeological or folkloric data; be wary of imputed meanings in later accounts and aim to show the 'clear truth of the setting' using multiple independent lines of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat commercial or partisan objections with scrutiny in international-technical policy debates
rubrics_metrics.description: When industry representatives alone raise objections to an international technical convention (e.g., mandatory intercommunication of radio-telegrams), assess whether technical objections are genuine or biased by private interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representatives of all other systems agree that intercommunication has no real technical difficulty, regard solitary technical objections with scepticism and weigh economic/monopoly motives; examine global station distributions and practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require anatomical or independent corroboration for physiological hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological theories (e.g., colour perception models) must seek corroboration from anatomy or other independent lines of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if psychophysical or theoretical arguments support a model (e.g., separate cone types), lack of anatomical evidence should be acknowledged and considered a limitation until corroborated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt systematic, well-documented fieldwork and reporting for archaeological surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic study of archaeological features (e.g., red-hills) requires thorough examination, clear reporting of sizes, distributions, and hypothesised functions, and publication of particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form joint committees when appropriate, examine representative sites thoroughly, illustrate findings (photographs, maps), and state aims clearly (e.g., to decide among salt-works, habitations, potteries hypotheses).
